episode_thesis: Graham's CIO argues that the ten-year post-GFC regime of accommodative central banks is over, and that the 2022-23 hiking cycle (record in speed and magnitude, and badly priced by markets) plus persistent core inflation makes stock-bond correlation near zero or positive, so 60/40 is more fragile. Macro strategies, with zero average but negative conditional correlation to equities and positive skew, are offered as a tactical complement to 60/40, and Graham's quant trend and quant macro programs and a bearish tactical stance (short equities, long euro, yen and gold) are described.

speakers.role: President and CIO of Graham Capital Management; oversees alpha development

worldview_premises.premise: For ten years after the GFC every shock was met by very accommodative central banks (zero lower bound, sticky-low inflation); that special regime ended with the 2022 inflation shock.
worldview_premises.support: Recollection of the taper tantrum and other episodes where the Fed backed off

worldview_premises.premise: An inflation shock must be met by a shock to real rates, so asset markets and central banks play a different game from the post-GFC decade.

Inflation is no longer seen as a secular low (supply disruptions, geopolitics, fiscal spending), so central banks will be shyer about accommodation even if inflation falls, bringing higher volatility and a harder time for 60/40.

In the four completed hiking cycles since Volcker the Fed stopped after turmoil; the 2022-23 cycle is the fifth and a record in speed and size (about double the average ~220bp in half the time, heading to about 500bp).
Markets are fragile to a hiking cycle to the degree that the forward curve at the first hike under-priced what the Fed then delivered.
worldview_premises.support: Own exercise comparing forward curves on day one of each cycle with the delivered path

worldview_premises.premise: The beta of asset returns to inflation is non-linear (helps in deflation, hurts in high inflation), which is why regressions look inconclusive; separating inflation by driver shows core inflation is a large negative shock while energy inflation is nearly unimportant because it is volatile and mean-reverting.
worldview_premises.support: Cites a Wharton study by two professors

worldview_premises.premise: Bonds are held to hedge: with an equity risk premium of 400-500bp, a lower-return bond only makes sense with low or negative correlation to stocks.

The long-run stock-bond correlation is about zero, an average of high positive (1960s-2000s, high inflation) and high negative periods; high inflation pushes it up and falling inflation pushes it negative.
worldview_premises.support: Cites a study on correlations; historical episodes

worldview_premises.premise: Newer market participants extrapolate 20 years of negative correlation (-0.5), which made 60/40 a bonanza and is not the long-run norm.

The 'stocks for the long run' case relies on mean reversion, but forward-looking variance must also estimate an unknown mean; with the lost degree of freedom, long-horizon equity volatility is about 22% rather than 17%, so mean-variance should hold fewer equities.
worldview_premises.support: Cites a Chicago study; variance 3% vs 5% arithmetic

worldview_premises.premise: Macro funds have zero average correlation to equities but negative conditional correlation (gain in large equity drawdowns) and positive skew, which matter more than Sharpe and standard deviation for portfolio construction.
worldview_premises.support: HFRI macro index charts and return distribution (almost 4 sigma upside, no -3 sigma)

worldview_premises.premise: Macro is a complement to 60/40: no long-term secular views (already in 60/40), tactical, dynamic and quick to cut positions when the thesis fails.
Fundamentals affect markets non-linearly and in a regime-dependent way, so linear signals are inadequate.
worldview_premises.support: Reasons given earlier for inflation non-linearity

decision_process.practice: Use macro as a complement to 60/40 with no secular view; adapt views frequently and cut positions as soon as the thesis does not work.
decision_process.why: Investors already hold secular exposure in 60/40

decision_process.practice: Risk management and a tactical hedge limit the cost of being wrong on the short equity view; risk systems are made more robust after the 20-sigma Treasury move of March 2023.
decision_process.why: Unknown market forces can support equities; shocks happen faster and more violently

decision_process.practice: Trend program: traditional time-series momentum signal with robust portfolio construction (mean-variance and PCA to estimate the covariance matrix quickly).
decision_process.why: Value added comes from portfolio construction on a standard signal

decision_process.practice: Quant macro program: four sub-strategies (trend, value/long-run reversion, carry, macro fundamentals) combined with mean-variance.
decision_process.why: More stable return profile than trend; Sharpe above one

decision_process.practice: Macro signal uses about 900,000 time series (GDP, inflation, earnings, inventories), NLP sentiment, data compression and non-linear regression.
decision_process.why: Fundamentals act non-linearly and by regime

decision_process.practice: Carry is not naive: the program estimates an equilibrium required carry and avoids simply buying high-carry assets.
decision_process.why: High carry is not always compensated

decision_process.practice: Quantitative portion of the absolute-return side is about 15% (trend plus quant macro programs).
decision_process.why: Reported share; see gaps for conflict with the host's statement

speakers.evidence_style: Historical comparison of hiking cycles, academic studies (Wharton, Chicago, correlation study), index-based backtests of a 60/40 plus macro mix, and firm track record claims; arguments are presented in a client-marketing setting.

current_views.view: Short equities: earnings must fall and multiples are too high; either sticky core inflation forces the Fed to hike against priced cuts, or core falls only through an unemployment spike and recession.
current_views.reasoning: Two likely scenarios both bad for equities; a hard landing would be terrible too.

current_views.view: Long euro: US banking issues keep the Fed from hiking massively while the ECB is hawkish.
Long yen: extremely undervalued, with a BoJ yield-curve-control change eventually coming.
Long gold (highest conviction): real rates are elevated and will come down, breakevens are too low, and the US debt ceiling negotiation is usually gold-bullish.
current_views.reasoning: Real rates, breakevens and debt ceiling history.

current_views.view: Stock-bond correlation will stay near zero rather than return to -0.5.
current_views.reasoning: Inflation is no longer a secular low.

current_views.view: Graham's trend program did very well in 2022, consistent with large macro dislocations; the March 2023 Treasury move barely affected Graham.
current_views.reasoning: Trend profits from dislocations; risk systems being hardened.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Corrected claim: the 'five hiking cycles' are four completed cycles (1994-95, 1999-2000, 2005-06, 2015-18) plus the still-running 2022-23 cycle; only the completed ones ended in turmoil and a Fed pause. The claim that 'each ended with crisis after which the Fed gave up' cannot apply to the current cycle.
Corrected claim: the description of trend as price-driven and quant macro as adding fundamentals was spoken by the host, not by Calderini.

The 20-year benefit of adding macro to 60/40 uses an industry index (HFRI macro) as the macro proxy, not Graham's own results, and the information ratio 0.66 to 0.75 and drawdown -36% to -29% are in-sample over a period when stock-bond correlation was negative; the claim of a larger benefit in stress years is not backed by figures.

The equity volatility adjustment (17% to 22%) comes from variance 3% to 5% with a study cited but not named; the result is asserted rather than shown, and the study's conclusion about stocks for the long run is contested.
Wharton and Chicago studies are cited without author names or dates.
Calderini calls March 2023 a 20-sigma Treasury event that hurt dynamic funds but says Graham was barely affected; no data supports Graham's resilience.

Share of Graham's business that is quantitative differs: the host says about two-thirds on the Quant side, while Calderini says about 15% of the absolute-return business is quantitative; the denominators differ and are not reconciled.
Quant macro 'running eight years' and 'trading since 2014' do not match in a 2023 recording (about nine years).

The short-equity thesis has both scenarios (sticky inflation, recession) plus a hard landing bearish for equities; the view is unfalsifiable except by Fed delivery against the priced cuts, and Calderini concedes forces beyond his understanding may support equities.

The gold case says breakevens can rise with unchanged rates so real rates fall; this requires inflation expectations to rise without a Fed response, which sits awkwardly with the main thesis of a hawkish Fed.
Calderini blames the Fed's communication for the 2022 shock yet also says 'either the Fed guided well or markets read it well'; the cause of the earlier match is not resolved.
The positive skew and negative conditional correlation of the macro index are described with a chart, but the fund-level sample, survivorship and fee effects are not discussed.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs said to lead prices: gap between forward-curve pricing and what the Fed delivers (cuts priced vs hikes), core inflation (services) and the unemployment rate as the route to lower core inflation, the sign of stock-bond correlation set by the inflation regime, real rates and breakevens (for gold), US banking stress and ECB/BoJ policy (for euro and yen), and the US debt ceiling. Horizon is weeks to a few months for tactical positions; the regime shift is multi-year.
reader_inferences: (reader) The core claim is regime-based: 60/40 worked because inflation was a low secular risk and correlation was negative; the testable implication is that macro's value to 60/40 should rise when stock-bond correlation is positive.
(reader) The 'fragility = unpriced Fed path' measure is a simple, replicable indicator (forward curve on day one versus delivered path) with only five observations.
(reader) The talk is an allocation pitch: macro's benefit (negative conditional correlation, positive skew) is presented with index data, and Graham's own record is referenced only qualitatively.
(reader) Tactical views (short equities, long euro, yen, gold) are explicitly changeable within a month, so they should not be treated as durable forecasts.
